related_questions.question: At what age does arthritis start?

text_blocks.snippet: Arthritis can start at any age, but generally, osteoarthritis (OA) is more common in people over 50, while rheumatoid arthritis (RA) typically develops between ages 30 and 50. However, both conditions can occur earlier in life due to factors like joint injury, overuse, or other underlying conditions.

list.snippet: RA typically appears between 30 and 50, but can affect people of all ages, including children.

list.title: Psoriatic Arthritis:
list.snippet: This type often shows up between ages 30 and 50, but it can also occur earlier.

related_questions.question: What's the best thing to do for arthritis?

text_blocks.snippet: The best approach to managing arthritis involves a combination of lifestyle adjustments, medication, and supportive therapies. This includes maintaining a healthy weight, engaging in regular exercise, and using heat or cold therapy. Medications like NSAIDs and corticosteroids, either oral or topical, can help with pain and inflammation. Physical therapy and assistive devices can also improve mobility and daily function.
snippet_highlighted_words: maintaining a healthy weight, engaging in regular exercise, and using heat or cold therapy

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed breakdown:
1. Lifestyle Changes:

list.title: Weight Management:
list.snippet: Losing weight can significantly reduce stress on weight-bearing joints, like knees and hips, alleviating pain and improving mobility.

list.title: Exercise:
list.snippet: Regular, low-impact exercise, such as walking, swimming, or cycling, can strengthen muscles around joints, improve flexibility, and reduce stiffness.

list.title: Heat and Cold Therapy:
list.snippet: Applying heat can relax muscles and ease pain, while cold therapy can reduce inflammation and numb pain, especially after physical activity.

list.title: Assistive Devices:
list.snippet: Using canes, walkers, or braces can provide support and reduce stress on affected joints.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: A healthy, balanced diet can help manage weight and reduce inflammation. Consider incorporating foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidants, while limiting processed foods, sugary drinks, and excessive salt.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. Medications:

list.title: Over-the-counter pain relievers:
list.snippet: NSAIDs like ibuprofen or acetaminophen can help reduce pain and inflammation.

list.title: Topical NSAIDs:
list.snippet: Creams and gels containing NSAIDs can be applied directly to the affected area, minimizing potential side effects of oral NSAIDs.

list.title: Corticosteroids:
list.snippet: These medications, including cortisone shots, can be used to reduce inflammation and pain.

list.title: Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs):
list.snippet: These medications are often used for rheumatoid arthritis to slow disease progression and reduce joint damage.

text_blocks.snippet: 3. Supportive Therapies:

list.title: Physical therapy:
list.snippet: Physical therapists can design exercise programs to improve strength, flexibility, and range of motion.

list.title: Occupational therapy:
list.snippet: Occupational therapists can help patients adapt their daily activities to minimize joint stress and improve function.

list.title: Acupuncture:
list.snippet: Some individuals find relief from arthritis pain through acupuncture.

list.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT):
list.snippet: CBT can help patients manage the psychological impact of chronic pain and develop coping strategies.

related_questions.question: Does arthritis hurt continuously?
related_questions.snippet: Pain from arthritis can be constant or it may come and go. It may occur when at rest or while moving. Pain may be in one part of the body or in many different parts.
related_questions.title: Do I Have Arthritis?

text_blocks.snippet: Early arthritis, also known as early-onset arthritis, can be caused by a variety of factors, including joint injuries, repetitive stress on joints, and genetic predisposition. While often associated with aging, arthritis can affect younger individuals due to these factors, especially those involved in high-impact activities or physically demanding jobs.
snippet_highlighted_words: joint injuries, repetitive stress on joints, and genetic predisposition

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed look at the causes:
1. Joint Injuries:

list.snippet: A history of joint injuries, such as sprains, dislocations, or fractures, can significantly increase the risk of developing arthritis, even years later.
These injuries can damage cartilage and other joint tissues, accelerating the wear-and-tear process.
Post-traumatic arthritis specifically refers to arthritis developing after an injury.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. Repetitive Stress and Overuse:

list.snippet: Engaging in activities that involve repetitive joint movements, like certain sports or physically demanding jobs, can put excessive stress on joints.
This repetitive stress can lead to cartilage breakdown and the development of osteoarthritis, even in young adults.

text_blocks.snippet: 3. Genetic Predisposition:

list.snippet: While not the sole cause, genetics can play a role in the development of arthritis.
Some individuals may inherit a genetic predisposition that makes them more susceptible to developing arthritis, even with relatively minor joint stress or injury.

text_blocks.snippet: 4. Other Factors:

list.title: Obesity:
list.snippet: Excess weight puts additional stress on weight-bearing joints, increasing the risk of osteoarthritis.

list.title: Infections:
list.snippet: Certain infections can trigger reactive arthritis, where the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the joints.

list.title: Smoking:
list.snippet: Smoking has been linked to an increased risk and severity of arthritis, potentially due to its impact on inflammation and joint health.

list.title: Certain Medical Conditions:
list.snippet: Some conditions like rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and psoriatic arthritis can develop at a young age, often with a genetic component or as a result of autoimmune responses.

text_blocks.snippet: 5. Age:

list.snippet: While early-onset arthritis is the focus, aging is still a significant factor in the development of osteoarthritis.
Over time, cartilage naturally wears down, making older adults more susceptible to osteoarthritis.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that the specific cause of arthritis can vary depending on the type of arthritis and individual circumstances. Early diagnosis and treatment can help manage symptoms and potentially slow down the progression of the disease.

text_blocks.snippet: Common symptoms of arthritis include joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and warmth or redness around the affected joint. These symptoms can vary in severity and may come and go. Other potential symptoms include limited range of motion, fatigue, and even fever or weight loss in some cases.
snippet_highlighted_words: joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and warmth or redness around the affected joint

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a more detailed breakdown:
1. Joint Pain: This is the most common symptom and can range from a dull ache to a sharp, intense pain. It may be constant or intermittent, worsening with activity or prolonged periods of rest.

2. Stiffness: Joint stiffness is particularly noticeable after periods of inactivity, such as in the morning or after sitting for a long time. It can make it difficult to move joints through their full range of motion.
3. Swelling: Inflammation around the affected joints can cause swelling, warmth, and tenderness to the touch.
4. Limited Range of Motion: Arthritis can restrict the flexibility and movement of joints, making it harder to perform everyday tasks.
5. Redness and Warmth: Redness and a feeling of warmth around the joint are signs of inflammation and can accompany swelling.
6. Fatigue: Many people with arthritis experience fatigue, a persistent feeling of tiredness and lack of energy.

7. Other Symptoms: Some types of arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, can also cause symptoms like fever, weight loss, and even affect other parts of the body, including the eyes, skin, lungs, and heart.
Specific to Osteoarthritis:

list.snippet: Bony Enlargement: In osteoarthritis, joints may become enlarged due to bone growth.
Crepitus: A grating or crackling sound or sensation in the joint during movement.

text_blocks.snippet: Specific to Rheumatoid Arthritis:

list.snippet: Symmetrical Pain: Symptoms often affect the same joints on both sides of the body.
Rheumatoid Nodules: Firm lumps under the skin near affected joints.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that these symptoms can vary in severity and presentation depending on the type of arthritis and the individual. If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, it's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.
